paras: The expulsion of Jim Myers from Newark Valley was the forced departure, in late May or early June 1881, of Jim Myers (also spelled Meyers) and, by one account, a French partner from their cabin at Antelope Springs, Nevada, after stockmen ordered them out under threat of lynching. The men left without violence, and Nevada papers treated the episode as a brief item of local news.

Myers and his partner had been living at Antelope Springs, where, according to the Eureka Leader, they were "in very bad repute among the cattle men on account of several little stock stealing affairs laid at their doors." No report gives the race of either man; the partner is identified only as "a Frenchman, whose name we did not learn."

The Eureka Leader, citing a rumor brought by a visitor from Newark Valley, reported that eight men visited the cabin and gave the two a week, "ending on last Saturday," to leave the valley "under penalty of lynching." They "took the hint" and were said to have left for Wood River.

The Hamilton correspondent of the White Pine News wrote instead that J. E. Meyers married Lizzie Borr on May 21 and that the next day a masked "committee" ordered him "to proceed on a wedding tour and not return"; he left, and Antelope Springs was "now deserted."
No arrest, charge or official response appears in the coverage, either over the alleged thefts or against the men who ordered Myers out.

The story reached the state press through the Eureka Leader, whose item the Silver State of Unionville paraphrased on June 8 among its "Sagebrush Screenings" and the Morning Appeal of Carson City reprinted on June 9 under the headline "Ordered Out by the Vigilantes."

The White Pine News carried its own correspondent's note on June 11 in a light tone, casting the expulsion as a forced "wedding tour" and adding that "cattle men in this end of the county sleep easier nights."

The accounts differ on the order's timing and form: the Eureka Leader described eight stockmen giving two men a week's notice, while the local Hamilton correspondent described a masked committee calling on Meyers alone the day after his May 21 wedding.

bases: Eight men, described by the Eureka Leader as stockmen and by the Hamilton correspondent as a masked 'committee', ordered Myers (and in one version his partner) to leave under threat of lynching, and he left; no one was reported harmed (A2, A3).
A group of eight stockmen or a masked committee threatened lynching over alleged stock stealing, but the men left and no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

The Eureka Leader item (reprinted in A1 and A2) and the independent Hamilton correspondence in the White Pine News (A3) agree that Meyers of Antelope Springs was ordered out by cattle men and left, though they differ on details.
